title: Gas smell
h1: Why does my car smell like gas?
metaDesc: Car smells like gas inside or outside? Answer a few questions to see if it's a loose gas cap, a vapor leak or a dangerous fuel leak, and what to do now.
synonyms: car smells like gas after filling up
smell gas when car is parked
car smells like gas when starting
car smells like gas but no leak
intro: A gas smell can be as simple as a loose gas cap or as serious as fuel leaking onto hot engine parts. What matters most is whether liquid fuel is leaking and whether the smell is strong inside the car. Answer the questions below to find the likely cause and the safest next step.
safety: If raw-fuel odor persists, the cabin smells strongly of gasoline or fuel is dripping, park safely and switch off the engine. Move away, leave the engine off, and arrange a tow.
If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.

q_where.q: Which of these best describes the gas smell?

opts.a: Fuel is dripping, or there's a wet spot under the car that smells like gas
It's strong inside the car while driving or idling
A faint smell outside the car, when parked or after starting

q_look.q: From where you were already standing, did you notice a wet spot or drip?
q_look.help: Use what you already noticed. Do not go back to look, lean over the engine or smell liquid to identify it.

opts.a: Yes, there's a wet spot or drip that smells of gas
No, everything looks dry but I still smell gas
The gas cap wasn't tight, or a check engine or gas cap light came on
Fuel splashed on the car, my shoes or my clothes
The pump nozzle keeps clicking off, or fuel overflows while filling
The smell lasts for hours, or there's a wet spot near the gas tank or filler

q_outside.q: Is the check engine light on, and where is the smell strongest?
q_outside.help: An engine light alone cannot distinguish a vapor-system fault from a fuel leak.

opts.a: The check engine light is on
No light. The smell is only at the tailpipe for a few minutes after a cold start
No light. The smell is around the engine or under the car

result.title: Fuel may be leaking from the car. This is a fire risk
result.now: If driving, pull over safely. Switch the engine off and leave it off. Move everyone away from the vehicle and any fuel, keep ignition sources away, and arrange a tow from a safe place. Do not search for the leak.
if: If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: Liquid gasoline gives off vapor that can ignite from a spark or a hot exhaust. A leak that drips while parked will usually get worse when the fuel system is under pressure with the engine running.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line
causes.clues: Drips along the underside of the car between the tank and the engine. Steel lines can rust through, especially in salted-road areas.

causes.name: Leaking fuel tank, filler neck or tank seal
causes.clues: The wet spot is under the gas tank or near the fuel filler.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: Wetness or a strong smell on top of the engine.

result.title: Fuel vapor is getting into the cabin, possibly from a leak
result.now: If driving, pull over safely. Switch the engine off and leave it off. Move everyone away from the vehicle and any fuel, keep ignition sources away, and arrange a tow from a safe place. Do not search for the leak.
if: If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.

For fuel on skin, move away from the spill and wash the exposed area with water and mild soap. If anyone inhaled fumes, get fresh air and call U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Call 911 for trouble breathing, collapse or inability to wake.
result.why: A strong gas smell inside means fuel vapor is building up where you're breathing and close to electrical parts. Common sources are a leak in the engine bay that gets pulled in through the vents, or a leak near the fuel pump access under the rear seat.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel line in the engine bay
causes.clues: The odor was noticeable near the vents or engine area before the vehicle was parked.

causes.name: Leaking fuel pump seal or tank fittings
causes.clues: The smell is strongest in the back seat area, often after a full fill-up.

causes.name: Spilled fuel or a leaking gas can in the car
causes.clues: You recently carried fuel or a lawn mower or generator.

result.title: A loose or worn gas cap is a common cause
result.now: Only if the odor was brief at the pump, has fully cleared and there is no spill or wet spot, secure the cap or capless filler as your owner's manual directs. If raw fuel odor remains, keep the engine off and arrange an inspection before driving.
if: If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If the odor returns or there is fuel on the ground, stay clear and arrange a tow. A steady warning light alone does not identify the cause.
result.why: The gas cap seals in fuel vapor. If it isn't tight or its seal is worn, vapor escapes and you smell gas around the car, and the car's leak check may turn on the check engine light. Capless fillers can be blocked open by dirt in the same way.

causes.name: Gas cap not tightened
causes.clues: You recently filled up and may not have heard it click.

causes.name: Worn or cracked cap seal
causes.clues: The rubber ring is hard, cracked or missing.

causes.name: Dirty capless filler flap
causes.clues: On cars without a cap, the flap doesn't close fully.

you: Tighten the cap until it clicks.
Check that the capless filler flap closes fully.
shop: EVAP smoke test if the light returns

result.title: Spilled fuel may be the source
result.now: Stop fueling, keep the engine off and move away from the spill. Notify the station attendant from a safe place. Do not get back in wearing fuel-soaked clothing. If fuel is pooling or there is a fire, move clear and call 911.
if: For fuel on skin, move away from the spill and wash the exposed area with water and mild soap. If anyone inhaled fumes, get fresh air and call U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Call 911 for trouble breathing, collapse or inability to wake.
If fuel soaked into the cabin, keep people out and get professional advice before using the vehicle.
result.why: Even a small splash of gasoline smells strong until it evaporates. Fuel on shoes, clothes or the car's paint near the filler can make it seem like the car is leaking.

causes.name: Fuel splashed while filling
causes.clues: The pump overflowed or dripped when you pulled the nozzle out.

causes.name: Fuel on shoes, clothes or floor mats
causes.clues: The smell is strongest near your feet and fades over time.

causes.name: A fuel leak instead
causes.clues: The smell doesn't fade, or there are wet spots under the car.
causes.against: If it fades within a few hours, a leak is less likely.

shop: Fuel system leak inspection if the smell doesn't go away

result.title: The fuel vapor system may not be venting properly while you fill up
result.now: Stop filling at the first automatic shutoff. Do not squeeze more fuel in or try another pump. If any fuel overflowed, leave the engine off, step away and notify the attendant. Repeated shutoff with room in the tank needs a filler and vent inspection before refueling again.
if: If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If fuel is still dripping after pumping stops, stay clear and arrange a tow when the area is safe.
result.why: As fuel goes in, the air and vapor in the tank must escape through the vapor system. If a vent valve or the charcoal canister is clogged, the vapor can't get out, so the pump keeps shutting off and fuel can spit back out of the filler.

causes.name: Clogged charcoal canister or vent valve
causes.clues: The pump clicks off over and over, and a check engine light may come on.

causes.name: Topping off past the first click
causes.clues: You often add fuel after the pump shuts off. This can flood the canister with liquid fuel.

causes.name: Kinked or blocked filler vent hose
causes.clues: The problem started after work near the gas tank or after hitting road debris.

result.title: The fuel filler neck or tank may be leaking. This can be a fire risk
result.now: If driving, pull over safely. Switch the engine off and leave it off. Move everyone away from the vehicle and any fuel, keep ignition sources away, and arrange a tow from a safe place. Do not search for the leak.
if: If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: A smell that lingers long after filling can mean fuel or vapor is escaping near the top of the tank or from the filler pipe. These leaks often show up only when the tank is full, because that's when fuel reaches the damaged spot.

causes.name: Rusted or cracked filler neck
causes.clues: Wetness or a strong smell behind the rear wheel on the filler side, worst after filling.

causes.name: Leaking fuel pump seal or tank fitting
causes.clues: The smell is strongest in the back seat or under the middle of the car, mostly when the tank is full.

causes.name: Loose or cracked vapor hose
causes.clues: A smell without any visible wetness.

result.title: A fuel smell needs checking even when the engine light is steady
result.now: If driving, pull over safely. Switch the engine off and leave it off. Move everyone away from the vehicle and any fuel, keep ignition sources away, and arrange a tow from a safe place. Do not search for the leak.
if: If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: Cars trap gas vapor from the tank in a charcoal canister and burn it in the engine later. If a hose, valve or seal in that system leaks, vapor escapes and the car's self-test turns on the check engine light. A code scan narrows down which part.

causes.name: Loose or worn gas cap
causes.clues: It started after a fill-up.

causes.name: Cracked EVAP hose or faulty purge or vent valve
causes.clues: An EVAP leak or valve code, and a smell near the tank or engine.

causes.name: Liquid fuel leak
causes.clues: Wet spots under the car or a strong smell that doesn't go away.

result.title: A brief fuel smell from the tailpipe on cold starts is often normal
result.now: Note how long the smell lasts after starting and mention it at your next service, or book a check when convenient if it's getting stronger.
if: If the smell lasts after the engine warms up, or you see black smoke, have it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine runs rough, get it checked soon.
If you smell raw fuel under the hood or under the car, not just at the tailpipe, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel, and the catalytic converter doesn't clean the exhaust until it heats up. That can leave a faint gas smell at the tailpipe for a minute or two. If the engine keeps running rich once warm, something is off with the fuel mixture.

causes.name: Normal cold-start enrichment
causes.clues: It fades within a few minutes and the car runs smoothly.

causes.name: Engine running rich
causes.clues: Worse gas mileage, black smoke, or a smell that lasts once warm.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector
causes.clues: Rough idle at startup, or a strong smell at the engine too.

you: Note whether the smell fades once the engine is warm.

result.title: There may be a small fuel or vapor leak. Have it found before driving
result.now: If driving, pull over safely. Switch the engine off and leave it off. Move everyone away from the vehicle and any fuel, keep ignition sources away, and arrange a tow from a safe place. Do not search for the leak.
if: If fuel is pooling or spreading, fumes are strong in an enclosed space, or you suspect a fire, get everyone clear and call 911 from outside the area.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: A gas smell with no visible puddle can come from a small seep that evaporates before it drips, or from a vapor hose. Small fuel leaks rarely fix themselves and can grow, and not seeing a drip doesn't rule out fuel reaching hot engine parts.

causes.name: Fuel injector seal or fuel rail seep
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the engine, especially right after starting.

causes.name: EVAP hose or canister leak
causes.clues: A smell near the gas tank, often stronger in hot weather.

causes.name: Seeping fuel line connection
causes.clues: Damp or stained areas along fuel lines underneath.
